power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Evidence-based psychotherapies benefit many patients, but individual outcomes vary and guidance for personalizing treatment remains limited.
The verbal theories underlying these treatments describe processes thought to produce improvement but often leave their strength, direction, functional form, and timescales unspecified.
This limits theory-informed predictions about how a particular patient would respond to alternative treatments.
Researchers have begun formalizing theories of psychopathology in mathematical or computational form to address these limitations.
Formal theories make theoretical assumptions explicit, allowing precise and testable predictions to be deduced analytically or through computational models.

When these models represent treatment effects and relevant individual differences, researchers can use patient measurements to inform model states and parameters, simulate alternative treatment configurations, and compare predicted outcomes.

Empirical evaluation must distinguish the accuracy of outcome predictions, support for the proposed mechanisms, and whether modelguided selection or adaptation improves outcomes relative to other treatment selection strategies.
Translating this potential into practice requires aligning the theory with patient assessment, treatment delivery, and evaluation.
We propose a roadmap for this process and describe conditions supporting the generation, delivery, and testing of formal theory-driven treatment recommendations.

A worked example using a formal theory of panic disorder and a modular digital therapy illustrates the roadmap's early phases, including provisional model extensions that generate different treatment predictions for two simulated patients.
We conclude by discussing challenges in theory development, patient matching, measurement, and empirical evaluation that must be addressed before these predictions can guide clinical care.
Evidence-based treatments benefit many patients, but outcomes vary considerably and many patients do not achieve clinically meaningful improvement (Cuijpers et al., 2021; Loerinc et al., 2015).

text.text: Therefore, clinicians are faced with a practical question: which treatment components should a specific patient receive, in what order, and at what dose?
Although clinicians already adapt treatment to individual needs, we currently have limited evidence-based guidance to inform these decisions (Cohen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Although clinicians already adapt treatment to individual needs, we currently have limited evidence-based guidance to inform these decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Data-driven approaches to precision mental healthcare address this question by using patient characteristics to predict outcomes under different treatments.
For example, the Personalized Advantage Index approach (DeRubeis et al., 2014) uses predictive models to compare a patient's expected outcomes under alternative treatments.
text.formatted: For example, the Personalized Advantage Index approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(DeRubeis et al., 2014)</ref> uses predictive models to compare a patient's expected outcomes under alternative treatments.

text.text: However, such approaches depend on data that support the treatment comparisons of interest, and detecting gains from individualized treatment selection can require samples larger than those available in many clinical trials (Luedtke et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, such approaches depend on data that support the treatment comparisons of interest, and detecting gains from individualized treatment selection can require samples larger than those available in many clinical trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Luedtke et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A further challenge arises when personalization concerns combinations, sequences, or doses of treatment components that were not varied in existing studies.
These are critical decisions for clinical practice, but their many possible configurations make direct empirical comparisons extremely challenging.
Formal theories offer a complementary way to generate treatment predictions.

While verbal theories describe processes thought to produce symptom improvement, they often leave their strength, functional form, and timescale unspecified, limiting the predictions that can be deduced.
Formal theories make these details explicit by expressing theorized mechanisms in mathematical or computational form (Robinaugh et al., 2024; Wang, Robinaugh et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Formal theories make these details explicit by expressing theorized mechanisms in mathematical or computational form <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Robinaugh et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Wang, Robinaugh et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When a formal model 1 represents how a treatment acts on the system and includes relevant individual differences, researchers can simulate how a hypothetical patient might respond to alternative configurations without first observing outcomes under every configuration (Ryan et al., 2025).

text.text: The resulting predictions can then identify candidate treatments and the mechanisms through which they are expected to work.

Related work has formalized clinical case formulations and combined them with patient data. Burger et al. (2020), for example, expressed an idiographic functional analysis in differential equations and simulated exposure and cognitive reappraisal.

text.text: The Prior Elicitation Module for Idiographic System Estimation (PREMISE) combines case formulations with personalized model estimation through prior elicitation and Bayesian updating (Burger et al., 2022).

Thus, the central challenge is how to translate these model-derived predictions into decisions for actual patients.

Currently, we can use formal models to simulate hypothetical patients, but we lack clear guidance on how to (1) match real-world measurements to simulations, (2) use the resulting theory-implied predictions to select and deliver interventions, and (3) evaluate the resulting predictions, the proposed explanation of response, and whether 1 Throughout, theory refers to the substantive explanatory account; formal theory refers to that account expressed in mathematical or computational form; and formal model or model refers to its mathematical or computational representation or implementation.

Here, we propose a roadmap for formal theorydriven personalization and illustrate this approach through a formal theory of panic disorder and a modular digital therapy.
This section describes several key elements for supporting formal theory-driven personalized treatments.

We use the term personalization to describe treatment decisions based on measurable patient-specific characteristics or processes, including relevant circumstances or contextual factors (Cohen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We use the term personalization to describe treatment decisions based on measurable patient-specific characteristics or processes, including relevant circumstances or contextual factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such decisions may concern which components a patient receives, their sequence, or their dose-for example, whether cognitive restructuring precedes exposure or how much exposure practice is assigned.
Formal theory-driven personalization offers a way to inform these decisions using predictions derived from explicitly represented mechanisms of psychopathology and treatment response.

Formal theory-driven personalization requires three things: (1) generating personalized treatment decisions from a formal model via simulation, (2) delivering the personalized treatment configurations in the real world, and (3) evaluating the resulting predictions, explanations, and clinical decisions empirically.
Achieving these aims will involve harmonizing the formal theory with a candidate treatment and assessment procedures.

Figure 1 illustrates connections among key elements that can inform the generation, delivery, and evaluation of personalized treatment decisions. the representation of individual differences in psychopathology and treatment processes with patient-to-model matching, treatment delivery, and empirical evaluation.

text.text: Together, these elements support decisions about treatment components, sequencing, and dosing.
Assessment
To compare treatment options, a formal theory should represent both the processes underlying psychopathology and how treatment components are hypothesized to change them (Figure 1, Panel A).
text.formatted: To compare treatment options, a formal theory should represent both the processes underlying psychopathology and how treatment components are hypothesized to change them (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, Panel A).

text.text: Because recovery from psychopathology may not simply reverse the pathway into disorder (Wang, Blanken, et al., 2026), a formal theory that explains onset or maintenance dynamics does not automatically explain treatment response, even when treatment components are included.
text.formatted: Because recovery from psychopathology may not simply reverse the pathway into disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Wang, Blanken, et al., 2026)</ref>, a formal theory that explains onset or maintenance dynamics does not automatically explain treatment response, even when treatment components are included.

text.text: The model should also accommodate individual differences in the hypothesized processes underlying psychopathology and treatment response, which can be represented through different initial states or parameter values within shared equations, rather than requiring a different model structure for every patient.
Supplementary Figure S2 distinguishes variation in states and parameters from variation in model structure.
text.formatted: Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref> distinguishes variation in states and parameters from variation in model structure.

text.text: For example, patients may differ in their willingness to attempt exposure or in the level of fear they believe they can tolerate before escaping.

Representing these differences would allow researchers to examine whether exposure schedules that begin with lower-or higher-intensity exercises are predicted to produce better outcomes for a given simulated patient.
To inform decisions for actual patients, measurements need to be linked to the model's variable component states and parameters (Figure 1, Panel B).
text.formatted: To inform decisions for actual patients, measurements need to be linked to the model's variable component states and parameters (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, Panel B).

text.text: Patient matching uses these observations to estimate plausible values for the quantities that differ between individuals, identifying settings under which simulated patterns approximate the patient's data.
For a real patient, the same observations may be consistent with several combinations of states and parameters.
The relevant question is whether these plausible representations imply meaningfully different treatment choices.

Depending on the quantities involved, matching may draw on questionnaire responses, repeated observations of symptoms and behavior, or features derived from passive data (e.g., collected via smartphone or wearable devices).
Researchers can then simulate alternative treatment configurations for the same patient and compare their predicted outcomes.
These comparisons may favor different configurations for different patients or for the same patient at different times.
The same treatment may also be favored across patients despite heterogeneity in predicted outcomes.
The treatment options compared in simulations also need to be deliverable in practice (Figure 1, Panel C).
text.formatted: The treatment options compared in simulations also need to be deliverable in practice (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, Panel C).

text.text: When predictions concern component selection, sequencing, or dosing, the treatment must allow those features to vary.
Additionally, the treatment's active elements and delivery procedures should correspond to those represented in the model.

Modular digital therapies offer one way to support this flexibility: standardized, standalone modules can be combined and sequenced differently across patients, with opportunities to vary the amount of between-session practice that is assigned (Cohen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Modular digital therapies offer one way to support this flexibility: standardized, standalone modules can be combined and sequenced differently across patients, with opportunities to vary the amount of between-session practice that is assigned <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cohen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers can use observations to support three related but distinct goals in formal theory-driven personalization (Figure 1, Panel D).
text.formatted: Researchers can use observations to support three related but distinct goals in formal theory-driven personalization (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, Panel D).

text.text: First, evaluating outcome predictions involves comparing predicted and observed outcomes, such as symptom change, without necessarily measuring every modeled process.

Second, evaluating the proposed explanation calls for observations of what patients receive, how they engage with active treatment elements, and how the targeted processes change (Cohen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Second, evaluating the proposed explanation calls for observations of what patients receive, how they engage with active treatment elements, and how the targeted processes change <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cohen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, examining an explanation based on disconfirming feared outcomes involves assessing expectations before exposure, what occurred during the exercise, and subsequent belief change.

Third, evaluating clinical utility requires testing whether using model-derived predictions to select or adapt treatment improves outcomes relative to a specified alternative decision strategy, such as clinician judgment, datadriven selection, or assigning the same treatment to all patients.
This requires a specified decision rule and a design that supports the comparison.
Within-treatment adaptation additionally requires timely observations to update predictions before the next decision.
These observations may overlap with those used to evaluate mechanisms but are selected for their relevance to the treatment decision.
We use the term personalization infrastructure to refer to the treatment-delivery and assessment capabilities supporting these goals.
Section 3 presents a roadmap for developing these capabilities and empirically evaluating the approach.
This section presents a roadmap for using formal theories to personalize psychological treatment.
The roadmap assumes that researchers have identified an existing formal theory they wish to use and a treatment they intend to deliver.
It addresses how to build on these starting points, rather than construct a formal theory from scratch.
The model and treatment may still require substantial development to represent relevant processes and deliver the configurations of interest.
Figure 2 presents four phases for developing and empirically evaluating formal theorydriven personalization.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> presents four phases for developing and empirically evaluating formal theorydriven personalization.

text.text: For each phase, we describe its purpose, the research tasks it involves, and what would justify proceeding or returning to earlier work.
We illustrate the early phases using the Panic Model and a modular digital therapy, while providing general guidance for remaining work.
An expanded roadmap and additional decision guidance are provided in the Supplement. indicate a typical progression through the four phases.

When returning to a previous phase, researchers should use abductive inference (Haslbeck et al., 2022), considering plausible explanations for discrepancies between what was expected versus what was observed to guide revision.

The purpose of this phase is to synthesize what is known about the formal theory and intended treatment, identifying whether they can support treatment personalization in alignment with the researcher's goals and where further work may be needed.
Researchers should examine the phenomena the theory aims to explain, the processes and individual differences it represents, and findings from existing simulations and empirical work.
Reviewing the computational implementation and reproducing available simulations can clarify how the model generates its reported behavior.
Treatment materials and delivery procedures should be considered alongside the model to identify how active elements and their formalized processes correspond (Cohen et al., 2023).

text.text: Before proceeding to Phase 2, researchers should document areas of alignment, explanatory shortcomings, and relevant processes missing from the model or treatment.
Our synthesis focused on whether prescribing different treatment configurations might benefit different patients receiving modular digital cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for panic disorder.
We reviewed the Panic Model (Robinaugh et al., 2024), its treatment implementation (Ryan et al., 2025), and the digital therapy's panic modules (Cohen et al., 2025; Craske & Barlow, 2022).

text.text: The original model reproduced individual differences in panic vulnerability and CBT efficacy in simulations but not moderate-severity panic disorder, and subsequent treatment simulations demonstrated heterogeneous responses.

The purpose of this phase is to determine whether the existing formal theory can support the intended treatment comparison and whether revisions are needed.

Before proceeding, researchers should establish that the model represents the relevant processes and reproduces the treatment-response phenomena identified for evaluation, and that any revisions preserve the phenomena already reproduced by the starting model.
Building on Phase 1, researchers should specify the treatment decision and a small set of phenomena the theory should explain.
Phenomena are robust, empirically established features of the world, such as variation in outcomes among patients receiving the same treatment.

Researchers should make the proposed explanation for these phenomena explicit, drawing on existing psychological theory, clinical knowledge, and empirical research (Fried, 2020; Haslbeck et al., 2022).

Failure to reproduce established treatment-response phenomena, or omission of processes needed to evaluate the comparison, is a different problem.

When such discrepancies arise, researchers should use abductive inference to consider whether they reflect parameter settings, auxiliary assumptions, or the proposed explanation (i.e., the theory) itself.
Revisions should faithfully represent the explanatory account, not simply produce different preferred treatments.
Researchers should evaluate the revised model against the intended treatment-response phenomena and the starting model's established successes.
If shortcomings remain, further theory development is indicated before interpreting its predictions.

We formalized an exposure willingness component, which represents a patient's readiness to attempt an exercise.
Exposure willingness is distinct from panic self-efficacy, which concerns general confidence in coping with panic.

Greater exposure willingness and panic self-efficacy increase the modeled probability of starting an assigned exercise, whereas greater expected distress, avoidance, and intensity of the assigned exposure decrease it.

Additionally, we formalized a package demand component to represent the additional burden of completing structured exposures involving preexposure planning and post-exposure processing, which lowers the probability of starting an assigned exercise.

Our worked example illustrates simulations of hypothetical patients, not validated digital twins of actual patients.
Formal theories offer a way to derive treatment predictions from explicit accounts of psychopathology and recovery.

Their clinical value depends on whether patients can be matched adequately, predicted treatments can be delivered, outcome and process predictions withstand empirical evaluation, and acting on those predictions improves care.
Progress will require testing and refining these links, including learning when further personalization is not supported.

The promise of this approach is therefore not personalization for its own sake, but a more explicit and testable basis for determining what treatment should be delivered, to whom, and when-and for learning when our theories are not yet sufficient to answer those questions.

Generating treatment predictions does not by itself specify how to select treatment.

Researchers must define which configurations are clinically appropriate and feasible, along with the objective and time horizon for comparing them, choices our worked example illustrates but does not settle.
Our worked example compared cumulative symptom burden over 12 weeks, rather than endpoint severity alone.

When researchers wish to evaluate many different potential treatments, doing so for every configuration may become impractical, creating a need for search procedures that can be checked against broader comparisons.
Selection also requires handling cases where predictions are effectively tied.
Here, considering patient preferences, burden, or feasibility may provide additional criteria.
Additionally, when uncertainty is large enough that it could reverse the ranking, selecting the configuration with the best point prediction may not be the most defensible choice.
Developing and evaluating procedures that handle these cases is a necessary step before simulated treatment predictions can become usable recommendations.
